analyst.report:
For query Q-0002, "Grain refinement still strengthens BCC multi-principal-element alloys at 1000 °C," the outcome is **insufficient in the sources searched**. No dataset was frozen, so no analysis was run and there is no verdict. The evidence level is 1 ("no dataset frozen").

**What was searched.** Two sources were searched, and both returned records:
- the MPEA dataset (Borg et al. 2020)
- the Texas A&M FCC dataset (Mulukutla et al. 2026)

The plan limited the scope to:
- multi-principal-element (high-entropy) alloys
- BCC phase class
- the elevated temperature band
- tension tests

The planned model was a Hall-Petch fit with alloy intercepts. Yield strength (MPa) was the outcome, and grain size (µm) was the predictor, transformed to its inverse square root.

**Why records were not usable.** Under the eligibility rules, 1543 records were out of scope and 96 had a missing value. Many records lacked key fields:
- **MPEA:** grain size was missing in 1308 records, test temperature band in 1545, test temperature in 181, test type in 395, yield strength in 478, ultimate tensile strength in 1006, and microstructure in 143.
- **Texas A&M FCC:** test temperature and ultimate tensile strength were each missing in 94 records, and yield strength in 1.

**Minimums not met.** A test needs all four fixed minimums to be met. None were:

| Minimum | Required | Found |
|---|---|---|
| Records | 30 | 0 |
| Groups | 10 | 0 |
| Alloys | 5 | 0 |
| Residual degrees of freedom | 10 | -1 |

**What a test would need.** Records of BCC multi-principal-element alloys tested in tension in the elevated temperature band, each reporting both grain size and yield strength. These would need to come from enough groups and alloys to reach the minimums above. Such records were not found in the sources searched.

analyst.report:
For query Q-0009, the outcome is sufficient in the sources searched, and the verdict is supported under the stated model, in the sources searched. The scope came from the fixed reference plan; the scope was not read from the claim, so parts of the scope, such as test conditions and which records count as in scope, were not stated by the claim itself. The pooled analysis used 97 records on 22 alloys in 20 groups. It gave a pooled estimate of 424.9 with a standard error of 64.4, which points in the direction the claim describes. The pooled result has p ≈ 1.3e-6 (approximate, nominal, one-sided), based on 20 informative papers, an effective number of papers of 3.94, a largest share of 38.7% and 19 degrees of freedom. The effective number of papers is a measure of how evenly the slope information is spread across groups. It is not a count of independent papers, and here it is much smaller than the number of groups, which means a few groups carry most of the information.

Two sources were searched. In the searched MPEA dataset, 76 records on 13 alloys in 19 groups gave an estimate of 424.1 with a standard error of 62.2, labelled agrees, with p ≈ 1.1e-6 (approximate, nominal, one-sided) and 19 informative papers, an effective number of papers of 3.93, a largest share of 38.7% and 18 degrees of freedom. Many MPEA records could not be used. For example, 1308 lacked grain size and 478 lacked yield strength. The searched Texas A&M FCC dataset contributed 21 records on 9 alloys, but they all fall in 1 group. Its estimate of 1173.3 therefore could not be used for inference on its own: inference was not valid because of insufficient groups, and it is labelled not enough data.

The sufficiency rule was the fixed minimum. Each minimum was met:
* Records: 97 against a minimum of 30 (met).
* Alloys: 22 against 5 (met).
* Groups: 20 against 10 (met).
* Residual degrees of freedom: 74 against 10 (met).

Minimums missed: none.

In the sensitivity checks, all 9 of 9 alternative sets agreed, with 0 conflicting and 0 short of data. Estimates ranged from 393.5 (without the group with the largest share of slope information) to 432.4 (scope not confirmed included). Dropping the group with the largest share left 89 records and gave an estimate of 393.5, with p ≈ 1.9e-4 (approximate, nominal, one-sided) and 19 informative papers, an effective number of papers of 3.24, a largest share of 52.1% and 18 degrees of freedom.

A simulation check is an important caution. Under estimated settings, the method's false-positive rate was 8.2% (from 7.1% to 9.5%) against a nominal level of 0.05. Detection was 97.5%. Under fixed settings, the false-positive rate was 8.9%, with detection of 100.0%. In both cases the conclusion was that the method is over-confident on this data structure under the stated assumptions. For this reason the p-values are best read as nominal and somewhat optimistic. The association holds under the stated model in the sources searched, but it does not show that smaller grains produce the higher strength. Evidence level: 6 (sufficient with a verdict).

analyst.report:
The outcome for this claim is sufficient in the sources searched, and the verdict is supported under the stated model, in the sources searched. Across both sources together, the pooled estimate of the slope linking yield strength to finer grain size is 424.9, with a standard error of 64.4, giving p ≈ 1.3e-6 (approximate, nominal, one-sided). This rests on 20 informative papers, an effective number of papers of 3.94, a largest share of 38.7% and 19 degrees of freedom. The effective number of papers describes how evenly the slope information is spread across groups. It is not a count of separate papers. The scope used here came from the fixed reference plan; the scope was not read from the claim, so the claim itself did not state the scope. The result is an association under the stated model, not a demonstration of the claim.

By source, the MPEA dataset gave an estimate of 424.1 (standard error 62.2, p ≈ 1.1e-6 (approximate, nominal, one-sided)). It used 76 records from 19 groups and 13 alloys, based on 19 informative papers, an effective number of papers of 3.93, a largest share of 38.7% and 18 degrees of freedom, and is labelled agrees. Many MPEA records could not be used: 1308 lacked grain size and 478 lacked yield strength. The Texas A&M FCC dataset gave an estimate of 1173.3, but it came from only 1 group, so inference was not valid (insufficient groups). That source is labelled not enough data.

The checks passed the fixed minimums. The analysis had 97 records against a minimum of 30, 20 groups against 10, 22 alloys against 5, and 74 residual degrees of freedom against 10. Minimums missed: none. Removing the group with the largest share of slope information gave 393.5 (p ≈ 1.9e-4 (approximate, nominal, one-sided), 19 informative papers, an effective number of papers of 3.24, a largest share of 52.1% and 18 degrees of freedom). Across 9 sensitivity sets, 9 agreed and 0 conflicted. The estimates ranged from 393.5 to 432.4.

A simulation check found a false-positive rate of 8.0% under fixed settings and 8.6% under estimated settings, at an alpha of 0.05. Under both settings, the method is over-confident on this data structure under the stated assumptions. The p-values should therefore be read as approximate and somewhat optimistic. The evidence level is 6, which corresponds to sufficient with a verdict.

The pooled slope estimate, which relates yield strength to grain size, is 424.9 with a standard error of 64.4 and p ≈ 1.3e-6 (approximate, nominal, one-sided). The effective number of papers describes how the slope information is spread across groups. It is not a count of independent papers. This is an association under the stated model. It does not show that grain size drives strength, and it does not prove the claim.

The sufficiency rule used was the fixed minimum. Records were met (minimum 30, found 97). Alloys were met (minimum 5, found 22). Groups were met (minimum 10, found 20). Residual degrees of freedom were met (minimum 10, found 74). Minimums missed: none.

That source gave an estimate of 424.1 (standard error 62.2, p ≈ 1.1e-6 (approximate, nominal, one-sided), 19 informative papers, an effective number of papers of 3.93, a largest share of 38.7% and 18 degrees of freedom), and its label is agrees. Many MPEA entries could not be used. For example, 1308 entries lacked grain size and 478 lacked yield strength.

The Texas A&M FCC dataset was searched but was labelled not enough data. It gave 21 records but only 1 group, so inference was not valid (insufficient groups).

Sensitivity checks also supported the result. Of 9 alternative data sets, 9 agreed, 0 conflicted and 0 lacked enough data. Estimates ranged from 393.5 ("without the group with the largest share of slope information") to 432.4 ("scope not confirmed included"). Dropping the group with the largest share of slope information gave 393.5 with p ≈ 1.9e-4 (approximate, nominal, one-sided) and 19 informative papers, an effective number of papers of 3.24, a largest share of 52.1% and 18 degrees of freedom.

Simulation checks raise a caution. With fixed assumptions, the false positive rate was 8.6% (range 7.4% to 9.9%). With estimated assumptions, it was 7.5% (range 6.4% to 8.8%). Both are above the nominal level of 0.05, and in each case the flag reads: the method is over-confident on this data structure under the stated assumptions. Detection rates were high, at 100.0% and 97.6%. For these reasons the p-values should be read as approximate.

runs.claim: In FCC multi-principal-element alloys, yield strength rises as grain size falls

analyst.report:
The claim is that in FCC multi-principal-element alloys, yield strength is higher when grain size is smaller. The outcome is sufficient in the sources searched, and the verdict is supported under the stated model, in the sources searched. The main cautions are these. The simulation check found the method over-confident on this data structure. The effective number of groups is small. A single group carries a large share of the slope information. So the nominal p-value should be read as more favourable than it really is.

The test fitted yield strength (MPa) as a baseline for each alloy plus one coefficient, shared by all alloys, times the inverse square root of grain size (µm); the estimate is that coefficient, in MPa·µm^0.5. The pooled estimate is 424.9 MPa·µm^0.5, with a standard error of 64.4 MPa·µm^0.5, giving p ≈ 1.3e-6 (approximate, nominal, one-sided); the estimate is positive, the direction the claim describes. The pooled fit used 97 records on 22 alloys, with 20 informative groups, an effective number of groups of 3.94, a largest share of 38.7% and 19 degrees of freedom. A group is a paper, or, for a source that is a single dataset, the whole dataset. The effective number of groups shows how concentrated the slope information is across groups. It is not a count of independent groups. The scope was set by the fixed reference plan and was not read from the claim.

Two sources were searched.

* **MPEA dataset:** This source supplied most of the data, with 76 records on 13 alloys from 19 groups. On its own it gave 424.1 MPa·µm^0.5 (p ≈ 1.1e-6 (approximate, nominal, one-sided)), which is in agreement with the pooled result. Many of its records could not be used because they lacked a needed field. For example, 1308 lacked grain size and 478 lacked yield strength.
* **Texas A&M FCC dataset:** This source supplied 21 records on 9 alloys. Because it is a single dataset, it counts as 1 group. It is therefore too few groups to test alone, and its own estimate of 1173.3 MPa·µm^0.5 is not a valid separate test (insufficient groups).

The sensitivity checks re-ran the test on 9 alternative data sets. 9 agreed with the pooled result and 0 conflicted. The estimates ranged from 393.5 MPa·µm^0.5 (without the group with the largest share of slope information) to 432.4 MPa·µm^0.5 (scope not confirmed included). Dropping the group with the largest share gave 393.5 MPa·µm^0.5 (p ≈ 1.9e-4 (approximate, nominal, one-sided)), with 19 informative groups, an effective number of groups of 3.24, a largest share of 52.1% and 18 degrees of freedom. This is still in agreement with the pooled result, but the information then becomes even more concentrated in one remaining group.

In the simulation check, with noise levels estimated from the data, the test was significant in 7.7% of simulations with no effect (6.6% to 9.0%, a 95% simulation interval covering simulation uncertainty only); with fixed illustrative noise levels, the test was significant in 8.5% of simulations with no effect (7.3% to 9.8%, a 95% simulation interval covering simulation uncertainty only), against a nominal level of 5.0%. Under both, the method is over-confident on this data structure under the stated assumptions. This means that when there is truly no effect, the test flags one more often than its nominal level of 5.0%. The check also gives detection rates when a real effect is present:

* With noise levels estimated from the data, the detection rate was 97.2%.
* With fixed illustrative noise levels, the detection rate was 100.0%.

A test requires fixed minimums: at least 30 records, 10 groups, 5 alloys and 10 residual degrees of freedom. The data provided 97 records, 20 groups, 22 alloys and 74 residual degrees of freedom, so every minimum was met and none was missed. Even so, the result describes an association under the stated model in the sources searched. It does not establish the claim. More independent groups with spread-out slope information would make the result less dependent on any one group.
